newsitem.title: INDIA: Indian cinema strike paralyses movie industry.
newsitem.headline: Indian cinema strike paralyses movie industry.

text.p: Film producers and distributors in India's movie capital of Bombay have lost hundreds of thousands of dollars since cinemas shut down on January 1 to protest agaist a steep tax hike, industry officials said on Wednesday.

"The industry is losing about 7.5 million rupees ($209,000) each day," said Balkrishna Shroff, one of Bombay's leading film distributors. "Even the government is losing about 3 million rupees daily in entertainment tax."
The indefinite strike was called to protest against plans by Maharashtra state, where Bombay is located, to levy a tax on cinema tickets that would double the price to the consumer.
Theatre owners say it would drive away their customers.
Bombay is the heart of India's movie industry, which every year churns out hundreds of Hindi films, full of lilting love songs, melodramatic villains and thrilling car chases.
For years, dozens of people have queued up outside Bombay theatres each day for their passports to three hours of enjoyment. Many willingly paid exorbitant black market rates.
Maharashtra has 1,300 theatres, 106 of them in Bombay.
But Bombay's theatres have worn a deserted look for the past week, with their foyers empty and display windows boarded up.
The strike has paralysed the production, distribution and exhibition sectors of the film industry, Shroff said, but he added film shooting continues.
Nearly a dozen films slated for release last December and in the first half of January have been delayed, he added.

"Maharashtra accounts for 25 percent of the whole country," Shroff said. "If distributors cannot guarantee such a large chunk, producers don't want to release their films. Hindi film releases have stopped not only in India but all over the world."
Prices of theatre tickets in Bombay's commercial district range from 40 rupees (just over US$1) to 100 rupees, but elsewhere in the state are rarely more than 25 rupees.
With theatre owners adamant that they will not reopen unless the state government backs off from its position, the stalemate seems set to continue indefinitely, strike leaders told Reuters.
"No, no, no, there is no alternative," said U.A. Thadani, the president of the Action Committee of the Film Industry. "We will not reopen until all our demands are agreed to."
Thadani said a compromise formula worked out by his committee in discussions with state Culture Minister Pramod Navalkar had been rejected by the government.
The government said it wanted the theatre owners to withdraw the strike before it would negotiate with them.
"The theatre owners must call off their strike before we can talk to them," Chief Minister Manohar Joshi told reporters.
The Maharashtra government says it originally relaxed tax rates to mark the centenary year of cinema in 1996. Now it wants to revert to the earlier rate because it is losing revenue.
"But the government actually earned 80 million rupees more in 1995-96, after it relaxed the tax," said Thadani.
